title: Trims, trails and scaling out
teaches: We buy the full size at one price with one stop and never add to it; we scale OUT: the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the stop moved to breakeven after it, and the rest trails a rising average; never average down; and what scaling out costs and what it buys.

facts.quote: In that case, you always want to buy fewer shares than you purchased in the initial breakout. That keeps you from running up your average purchase price too much.
facts.claim: When you add to a stock you already own, IBD buys fewer shares than the first breakout buy, so the average cost doesn't run up too far.

facts.quote: You can use those entries to add to your existing position or, in some cases, initiate a new one.
facts.claim: A later buy point in a winning stock can be used to add to a position you already hold.

facts.quote: Make sure the stock bounces off the moving average line and heads higher on heavy volume You want the stock to rebound and show strength, not weakness, before you buy.
facts.claim: On a pullback add, IBD waits for the stock to bounce and head higher on heavy volume before buying.

facts.quote: Never buy a stock as it's moving down.
facts.claim: IBD's rule: never buy a stock while it is falling.

facts.quote: Look for light volume on the pullback This shows professional investors are not aggressively selling shares.
facts.claim: IBD wants light volume on a pullback, a sign big investors are not selling hard.

facts.quote: Though contrary to human nature, the best way to sell a stock is while it's on the way up, still advancing and looking strong to everyone.
facts.claim: IBD sells into strength: while the stock is still rising and looks strong.

facts.quote: So after a significant advance of 20% to 25%, sell into strength.
facts.claim: IBD's own profit-taking zone is a 20% to 25% advance.

facts.quote: What about the 'averaging down' strategy of buying more shares in a stock if the price drops? My advice is, don't do it
facts.claim: O'Neil's advice on buying more of a stock after it drops: don't.

facts.quote: it is throwing good money after bad. The only averaging that makes sense is 'averaging up' in your purchasing.
facts.claim: O'Neil calls averaging down throwing good money after bad; the only averaging he accepts is averaging up.

facts.quote: The best time to sell and take your profit is when your stock is advancing and still looks strong and positive to most investors.
facts.claim: O'Neil takes profits while the stock is still rising and looks strong.

facts.quote: If you buy later when a stock is 10%, 20% or 30% extended from a sound chart base, you will be shaken out on minor 8% pullbacks in price much more frequently.
facts.claim: Buying a stock that is already extended gets you shaken out on normal pullbacks far more often.

facts.quote: Figure 2: Bad behavior - The 7 deadly sins to avoid Averaging down into losing positions
facts.claim: Hirsch lists averaging down into losing positions first among the deadly sins of managing positions.

facts.quote: Most of us have trouble admitting we were wrong and tend to buy more of a stock that has fallen, under the guise that it's cheaper
facts.claim: Buying more of a falling stock because it looks cheaper is often a way of not admitting you were wrong.

facts.quote: is to sell half on a double. This way you take your initial investment off the table and you let your winnings ride.
facts.claim: Hirsch's rule: when a stock doubles, sell half to take your original cost out and let the rest ride.

facts.quote: when they are extended in the short term you can reduce your holdings to a two-thirds or even one-third position.
facts.claim: When a holding gets extended short term, Hirsch trims it to a two-thirds or even one-third position.

facts.quote: Selling too soon can be almost as detrimental to long-term returns as money-losing trades. This is why it can be important to harvest gains and then set trailing stop losses.
facts.claim: Selling a winner too early hurts too, so harvest some gains and then trail a stop on the rest.

facts.quote: You can set profit and loss targets from a purchase price. For example, a rule could be a 2:1 or 3:1 profit/loss target.
facts.claim: One exit rule Fidelity gives as an example: a profit target two or three times the planned loss.

facts.quote: Or if your stock is moving sharply higher, consider selling a portion of your position, while letting the remainder ride to capture any further gains.
facts.claim: When a stock runs sharply higher, sell part of the position and let the rest ride.

facts.quote: when an investor can start off their trade with smaller trade sizes and only add to a trade when it's winning, they are able to start off the trade by risking a little
facts.claim: Start smaller and add only when the trade is winning, and you begin by risking a little.

facts.quote: it also reduces risk by starting with a smaller trade, only adding to the trade after it's profitable.
facts.claim: Starting small and adding only after the trade is in profit lowers the risk of the first stage.

facts.quote: Rather than closing out an entire position once a target price is reached, an investor will partially close the trade in increments, allowing the rest of the shares to ride the stock's move further into profitable territory.
facts.claim: Scaling out means closing a trade in pieces so the rest of the shares can keep riding.

facts.quote: It is also common to move your stop loss to break even or beyond when an initial profit target is hit. That way, the remaining position you have open is almost 'risk-free.'
facts.claim: Moving the stop to breakeven after the first target is common, and Investopedia itself only calls the rest almost risk-free.

facts.quote: Average up refers to the process of buying additional shares of a stock that an investor already owns, but at a higher price. This raises the average price that the investor has paid for all their shares.
facts.claim: Averaging up is buying more of a stock you own at a higher price, which raises your average cost.

facts.quote: Investors following an average-up strategy could expose themselves to increased losses if they wind up buying company shares just before they fall sharply or if the stock price hits a peak.
facts.claim: Adding to a winner raises what you lose if the stock then turns down hard.

facts.quote: Averaging down is an investment strategy where an investor buys additional shares of a stock after its price has fallen, thereby reducing the average cost per share.
facts.claim: Averaging down is buying more after the price has fallen, which lowers your average cost.

facts.quote: who bought 100 shares of a stock at $50 per share might purchase an additional 100 shares if the price of the stock reached $40 per share, thus bringing their average price (or cost basis) down to $45 per share.
facts.claim: 100 shares at $50 plus 100 at $40 gives an average cost of $45.

facts.quote: The problem with averaging down is that the average investor has very little ability to distinguish between a temporary drop in price and a warning signal that prices are about to go much lower.
facts.claim: Most people can't tell a temporary dip from the start of a much bigger drop.

facts.quote: Adding more to a position, however, increases overall risk exposure
facts.claim: Buying more of a falling stock raises your total exposure to it.

facts.quote: Pyramid trading starts with a small position, adding more when the asset performs well and shows growth potential.
facts.claim: Pyramiding adds to a position as it performs well.

facts.quote: The use of profits on existing positions as margin to increase the size of the position, typically in successively smaller increments.
facts.claim: Pyramiding uses a position's profits to grow it, usually in smaller and smaller pieces.

facts.quote: Scaling out means selling not thy whole wad at one time, but selling only a portion of your holdings each time.
facts.claim: Scaling out is selling a position in portions rather than all at once.

facts.quote: If you want to make less profit, then scale out of a trade.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's summary of his tests: scaling out makes less profit than selling the whole position at once.

facts.quote: In the first test, I bought 200 shares at 10 and sold it all at 15 (buy & hold), giving me a profit of $980 after deducting $20 for round trip
facts.claim: Bulkowski's first test: 200 shares bought at 10 and all sold at 15.

facts.quote: Scaling out half of the position (100 shares) midway to the 15 target gives a profit of $720. Scaling out is worse.
facts.claim: Selling half midway to the target made less than holding all of it to the target.

facts.quote: Price climbs from 10 to over 12.50 but does not reach 15. This time, though, your stop is at the entry price of 10 (break even), so you lose the cost of commissions
facts.claim: Bulkowski's third test: the stock rises past 12.50, then falls back to a breakeven stop at 10.

facts.quote: Scaling out, however, means you sell half your holdings at 12.50 and the rest at 10 for a gain of $220. Scaling out works better in this scenario.
facts.claim: When the stock comes back to the stop, the partial sale is what made money.

facts.quote: Swing trader Probably not. If you're too early, expecting a turn and the stock is continuing to drop, then average down if market and industry are rising and do so only once.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's answer for swing traders on averaging down: probably not, and never more than once.

facts.quote: If you want to average down a second time, sell the loser instead. Remember, you're supposed to be a pro. Admit your mistake, take the loss, and move on.
facts.claim: If you're tempted to average down again, sell the loser and move on.

facts.quote: Price has to rise after you average down.
facts.claim: Averaging down only helps if the stock turns back up.

facts.quote: I almost never average down on my trading positions. All that does is make the loss grow when you throw in the towel and sell just days before price turns higher.
facts.claim: Bulkowski almost never averages down on trades: it makes the loss bigger.

facts.quote: Others like to buy more stock as additional trading signals occur when price rises.
facts.claim: Some traders buy more as new buy signals appear while the price rises.

facts.quote: If price is higher than the previous buy or the weighted average buy price, it's called averaging up.
facts.claim: Buying more above your earlier buy or your average price is averaging up.

facts.quote: according to an article in the October 2009 issue of Active Trader magazine titled, "Scaling in as an entry technique," by Howard Bandy, the technique lowers profit.
facts.claim: Bulkowski reports Howard Bandy's finding (Active Trader, October 2009) that scaling in lowers profit.

facts.quote: Insider Tip #2: Adding to a position isn't free upside. It's a whole new setup.
facts.claim: An add is not free upside; it is a whole new setup.

facts.quote: Are you going to risk the same amount, go lighter, or go heavier? Whatever you decide, treat this as a new trade.
facts.claim: Size an add as a new trade, with its own risk decision.

facts.quote: And if your original entry point is still close, meaning you might lose some profit or take a smaller loss if you get stopped out, you will have to take that position into consideration.
facts.claim: When you add, work out what the whole position does at the stop, old shares and new.

facts.quote: Dividing your risk-per-trade by your risk-per-share tells you exactly how many shares you can hold in your position.
facts.claim: Shares equal the dollars you risk divided by the risk per share.

facts.quote: the risk of amplified losses that may occur from having a large portion of your holdings in a particular investment, asset class or market segment relative to your overall portfolio.
facts.claim: A big position in one stock amplifies the loss when it falls.

facts.quote: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached. The price you receive upon execution, though, could be markedly different than your stop price.
facts.claim: A triggered stop is a market order, and the fill can be far from the stop price.

facts.quote: Dollar-cost averaging means investing your money in equal portions, at regular intervals, regardless of the ups and downs in the market.
facts.claim: Dollar-cost averaging is equal amounts on a schedule, whatever the price does.

facts.quote: If you're more concerned about protecting your profits than you are about potentially getting stopped out, consider using a trailing stop
facts.claim: When protecting profits matters more to you than getting stopped out, Schwab suggests a trailing stop.

facts.quote: Hold your winners by selling partials into strength and trailing the rising moving averages.
facts.claim: Our rule for winners: sell partials into strength and trail the rest under the rising moving averages.

facts.quote: The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: Our first trim, the hard rule: a third of the position at 3R. In practice the owner often waits for 5R.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally.
facts.claim: Our stop moves up to breakeven once the trade is 2R to 5R ahead; we teach it at the first trim.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: After the first third at 3R, we sell another third at 5R and trail the last third.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our trail is the 10-day average for fast movers or the 21-day for steadier ones; a close below it sells the last third.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: If the stock opens above a trim level, we take that trim at the open.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: Our time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: When a stock gaps down through our stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: If the first 30 minutes of the gap day already put the loss past 2R, we get out.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: Our entries are market orders.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: Our rule: the whole position goes on at one price with one stop, and we never add to it.

facts.quote: I do not scale into trade i buy full at one spot with one stop.
facts.claim: The owner's words: he does not scale in; the full size goes on at one spot with one stop.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: Our stop only moves up, never down or wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: Every position carries a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: After a stop-out we buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop.

facts.quote: New trims rules are what I like for hard rule can say trim 1/3 at 3R but I rarely actually do that and mostly wait for 5R.
facts.claim: The owner's words on the first trim: a third at 3R is the hard rule, though he mostly waits for 5R.

facts.quote: The first sell is a judgment that depends on a variety of factors, not a fixed third at 3R.
facts.claim: The owner's ruling: the first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.

facts.quote: He very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy; he usually waits until day 3 at the earliest.
facts.claim: The owner rarely sells on day 1 of the buy and usually waits until day 3 at the earliest.

facts.quote: Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best.
facts.claim: The owner's ruling: selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best.

walkthroughs.title: Add only to a winner
steps: You can build a position in steps. Each new step comes only after the last one is working.
Adding to a loser is averaging down. O'Neil's advice on that was simple: don't do it.
Every add is a new trade. It gets its own stop and its own size.

walkthroughs.title: What an add does to your numbers
steps: Buy more above your first price and your average cost goes up.
IBD buys fewer shares on an add than on the first buy, so the average doesn't run up too far.
More shares also means a stop-out costs more. Check what the whole position loses at the stop before you add.

walkthroughs.title: Scaling out, and what it costs
steps: Scaling out means selling part of a winner and letting the rest ride.
Our way: the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later. Stop to breakeven; the rest trails a rising average.
It isn't free. In Bulkowski's tests, scaling out made less when the stock ran all the way.
It pays when the stock comes back before your target. You're trading some upside for a gain in hand.

walkthroughs.title: One price, one stop
steps: We buy the full size at one price, with one stop. No starter piece, no adding as it works.
The size is set before the buy, from the stop, and goes in as one market order.
What we scale is the exit: a first sell by judgment, usually day 3 or later, then a trail.

questions.q: You own a stock and buy more shares at a higher price than you paid before. What's that called?
questions.why: Averaging up. It means buying more shares of a stock you already own, at a higher price than before. That raises your average cost per share. Averaging down is the reverse: buying more after the price falls. We do neither. Our rule puts the full size on at one price, with one stop.
questions.lesson_line: Buying more of a winner at a higher price is averaging up.

wrong.Averaging down: That's buying more after the price falls below what you paid.
wrong.Dollar-cost averaging: That's investing equal amounts on a schedule, whatever the price does.
wrong.Scaling out: That's selling part of a position, not buying more.

questions.simple: Averaging up. You buy more of a stock you already own, at a higher price than your first buy.

questions.q: Pyramiding means buying more of a stock as it falls below your first buy.
questions.why: False. Pyramiding adds to a position as it performs well, usually in smaller and smaller pieces. Buying more as a stock falls below your first buy is averaging down. That lowers your average cost instead. We do neither: the full size goes on at one price, with one stop.
questions.lesson_line: Pyramiding means adding to a winner. Adding to a loser has another name: averaging down.
questions.simple: False. Pyramiding means adding to a stock that is working, while buying more as it falls is averaging down.

questions.q: Averaging down on a losing trade is the same thing as dollar-cost averaging.
questions.why: False. Dollar-cost averaging puts equal amounts in at regular intervals, whatever the price does. Averaging down buys more of a stock because it fell below your price, which lowers your average cost. One is a schedule set in advance. The other is a reaction to a loss. A schedule can still buy on a dip, but that does not make them the same.
questions.lesson_line: A schedule is a plan. Averaging down is a reaction to a loss.
questions.simple: False. Dollar-cost averaging buys on a set schedule, while averaging down buys more because the price fell below yours.

reasons: stable definitions, a Tier 1 SEC fact plus Investopedia

questions.q: Finish O'Neil's rule.
questions.sentence: The only averaging that makes sense is averaging ___.
questions.why: Up. O'Neil's advice on averaging down was simple: don't do it, because it is throwing good money after bad. The only averaging he accepted was averaging up. Hirsch lists averaging down into losing positions among the deadly sins of managing positions. Our own rule goes further. The full size goes on at one price with one stop, and we add in neither direction.
questions.lesson_line: O'Neil's rule: average up, never down.
questions.simple: Up. O'Neil said never average down, and the only averaging that makes sense to him is averaging up.

reasons: the why adds the owner's rule A5 (no adding)

questions.q: Adding to a winner at a higher price raises your average cost per share.
questions.why: True. Every share you buy above your average pulls the average up. IBD keeps adds smaller than the first buy so it doesn't run up too far.
questions.lesson_line: Adds raise your average cost. Keep them small so it stays close to your first buy.

questions.q: You sell part of a winning position at a gain and let the rest keep running. What's that called?
questions.why: Scaling out. You close a trade in pieces instead of all at once, so the shares you keep can ride the move further. Pyramiding goes the other way: it adds shares. Stopping out is your stop being hit, not a planned sale. When we sell the first piece is a judgment, usually day 3 or later, and the rest rides a trail.
questions.lesson_line: Scaling out: sell some, let the rest ride.

wrong.Stopping out: That's your stop getting hit, not a planned sale into a gain.
wrong.Averaging down: That's buying more after a drop, not selling.
wrong.Pyramiding: That's adding shares to a winner. It goes the other way.

questions.simple: Scaling out. You sell part of a winner and let the rest of the shares keep riding.

questions.q: Finish our rule for holding winners.
questions.sentence: Hold your winners by selling partials into ___ and trailing the rising moving averages.
questions.why: Strength. Our rule: hold winners by selling partials into strength and trailing the rising moving averages. You sell part while the stock is still rising and looks strong, not after it rolls over. IBD and O'Neil teach the same timing: sell while it is advancing and still looks strong. IBD says this runs contrary to human nature.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. The rest rides on a rising stop.
questions.simple: Strength. We sell part while the stock is still rising and looks strong, not after it turns down.

reasons: rests on the owner's rule (sizing_rule.md section 6, A11)

questions.q: You own 300 shares at $40. You add 100 shares at $44. What's your new average cost per share?
questions.why: $41. The 100-share add is a third the size of your first buy, so your average only moves a little toward $44.
questions.lesson_line: A small add barely moves your average cost. That's why IBD keeps adds smaller than the first buy.

questions.q: How does our plan decide the first sell?
choices: A judgment, usually from day 3 on
A fixed third at 3R every time
Half of it, once the stock doubles
questions.answer: A judgment, usually from day 3 on
questions.why: A judgment, usually from day 3 on. The first sell depends on a variety of factors, not a fixed third at 3R. He very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy and usually waits until day 3 at the earliest. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best. R is only the measuring stick: your entry minus your stop.
questions.lesson_line: First sell: a judgment, usually day 3 or later. R is the ruler, not the trigger.

wrong.A fixed third at 3R every time: That was the old rule. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
wrong.Half of it, once the stock doubles: That's Hirsch's rule for a stock that doubles. Ours is a judgment, not a set rule like that.
wrong.Some once up 20% to 25%: That echoes IBD's profit-taking zone. Ours ignores a set percent and follows how the trade is working.

questions.simple: A judgment call, usually from day 3 on, because it depends on the trade and not on one fixed price.

questions.q: Your full plan is 400 shares, stop $2 under entry. You start with 100 and the stop hits before you add. What do you lose?
questions.why: $200, if it fills at your stop. Only the 100-share starter was on, not the full 400. The flip side: if it runs at once, you own less of the move.
questions.lesson_line: Start small and the trade has to prove itself before your full size is on.

questions.q: Once your trade shows a profit, an add on top of it carries no real risk.
questions.why: False. An add is a whole new setup with its own risk. If the stock turns, the new shares lose, and they can eat the gain on your first shares.
questions.lesson_line: A profit on your first shares doesn't protect the new ones.

questions.story: You bought at $50 with a stop at $47. It's now $47.50 and still sliding. A friend says buy more here to lower your average.
questions.q: How do you respond?
choices: Stick to the stop, add nothing
Hold, but lower the stop to $45
Buy more right at the stop
questions.answer: Stick to the stop, add nothing
questions.why: Stick to the stop and add nothing. Buying here puts more money behind a trade that is proving you wrong. O'Neil called averaging down throwing good money after bad. A lower average also means a bigger position in a falling stock. Our rule is plain: we never add, and the stop only moves up, never down. If $47 hits, you're out.
questions.lesson_line: Never add to a loser. The stop is the plan.

wrong.Buy more, it's cheaper now: Cheaper isn't better. Most of us can't tell a dip from the start of a much bigger drop.
wrong.Hold, but lower the stop to $45: That widens the loss you planned. Our stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Buy more right at the stop: If $47 hits, you're out anyway, now with more shares and a bigger loss.

questions.simple: Stick to the stop and add nothing. Buying more puts more money into a trade that is proving you wrong.

deeper.trap: The friend's math is right: more shares at $47.50 do lower your average. That is the trap. A lower average only helps if the stock turns back up. Most people can't tell a temporary dip from the start of a much bigger drop. The extra shares make that bigger drop cost more.

questions.q: You bought 100 shares at $50. At $40 you buy 100 more. What price gets you back to break even?
questions.why: Your new average cost is the total spent divided by the total shares. 100 shares at $50 and 100 at $40 average out to $45. The bar to break even came down. But now twice the shares ride on a stock that has been falling. We don't average down: the full size goes on once, with one stop.
questions.lesson_line: Averaging down lowers the bar and raises the bet. The stock still has to turn.
questions.simple: $45. That is your new average cost, so the stock only has to climb back to $45 to break even.

wrong.$50.00: That is your first price. The second buy lowered your average.
wrong.$40.00: That is only the second price. Your average includes both buys.
wrong.$90.00: Added the two prices and forgot to divide by the number of buys.

questions.q: You just sold part of a winner. What's the plan for the shares you kept?
choices: Let them ride on a trailing stop
Keep the original stop under them
Buy more on the next dip
Hold them with no stop at all
questions.answer: Let them ride on a trailing stop
questions.why: Let them ride on a trailing stop. The partial banks some gain, and the rest stays on for more of the move. Hirsch's version: harvest gains, then set trailing stops. Ours: the stop goes to breakeven at the first trim, and the last third trails the 10-day or 21-day average. The stop rises as the stock does.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some, then trail the rest. The stop rises as the stock does.

wrong.Keep the original stop under them: On a winner, that stop sits well below. Our stop moves up to breakeven at the first trim, so a reversal costs far less.
wrong.Buy more on the next dip: We don't add to a position. The shares you kept have one job: ride the trail.
wrong.Hold them with no stop at all: A winner can still reverse. The rest needs a stop that rises with it.

questions.simple: Let them ride on a trailing stop. The sale banks some gain, and the rest stays on for more of the move.

questions.q: You bought 100 shares at $30. It doubles to $60. How many shares do you sell to get your whole cost back?
questions.why: Your cost is the 100 shares you bought at $30. At $60, each share is worth twice what you paid. So half the shares bring back your whole cost. That is Hirsch's rule: sell half on a double and let the rest ride. It is his rule, not ours. Our first sell is a judgment, usually on day 3 or later.
questions.lesson_line: Half on a double gets your cost back. The rest rides on the gain.
questions.simple: 50 shares. At $60 each share is worth twice what you paid, so selling half gets your cost back.

wrong.100 shares: Divided your cost by the $30 entry price. Use today's $60 price.
wrong.30 shares: Used the $30 entry price as a share count.
wrong.25 shares: Halved twice. Half the shares, not a quarter, return the cost.

questions.q: A stop moved up to your breakeven can still lose you money on the shares you kept.
questions.why: True. A stop order becomes a market order once its price is reached. The fill can be markedly different from the stop price. So a breakeven stop order can fill below your entry when a stock gaps down through it. Even Investopedia calls the rest only almost risk-free.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven on paper isn't breakeven in a gap.
questions.simple: True. A stop order turns into a market order, so a gap down can fill it below breakeven.

deeper.trap: Breakeven on paper is not breakeven in a gap. A stop order at your entry only names the price that starts the sale. If the stock opens below it, the market order fills at whatever the market pays at that moment.

reasons: Tier 1 FINRA quote reconfirmed on its page 2026-11-12

questions.q: Entry $40, stop $38. Our plans put the first trim at 2R. What price is that?
questions.why: $44. One R is your entry minus your stop. Two of those above your $40 entry is the first trim.
questions.lesson_line: Trims are measured from your own risk. Know the 2R price before you buy.

questions.q: You bought 100 at $50, stop $48. At $55 you add 100 and leave the stop at $48. What does the whole position lose at the stop?
questions.why: $900, if it fills at $48. The add from $55 rides all the way down to $48 too. Leaving the stop where it was turned a small risk into a big one.
questions.lesson_line: Before you add, check what the whole position loses at the stop, not just the new shares.

questions.story: You buy 200 shares at $10, then sell 100 at $12.50 and 100 at $15. A friend buys 200 at $10 and sells all 200 at $15.
questions.q: Leaving out commissions, who made more?

args.expr: s * (top - entry) - h * (part - entry) - h * (top - entry)

questions.why: Your friend, by $250. Your first 100 shares stopped earning at $12.50. Your friend's kept earning all the way to $15. When a stock runs all the way to the target, scaling out makes less. Bulkowski's first test found the same. That is the cost of a gain in hand.
questions.lesson_line: Scaling out gives up some of a big run. That's the price of a gain in hand.

wrong.Your friend, by $500: That's double the gap. Only your first 100 shares sold early, at $12.50.
wrong.You did, by selling early: Backwards. Selling early capped the gain on half your shares.
wrong.The same profit for both: Only if you'd sold both halves at $15. You sold one at $12.50.

questions.simple: Your friend made $250 more. Your first 100 shares stopped earning at $12.50 while the friend's kept going to $15.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging scaling out by this one ending. Here the stock ran all the way to the target, so the partial cost you. A trade that turns back before the target is a different story, so scaling out is a trade-off, not free profit.

questions.story: You own a winner that broke out a few weeks ago. It's pulling back toward its 50-day moving average. Today it's still falling, on rising volume.
questions.q: You want to add. When do you buy?
choices: After it bounces and turns up
Buy the dip while it's falling
Add today with a wider stop
Double up to catch the low
questions.answer: After it bounces and turns up
questions.why: After it bounces and turns up. IBD's rule: never buy a stock as it's moving down. IBD also wants light volume on a pullback, and this one is on rising volume.
questions.lesson_line: Add on strength, never into a falling stock.

wrong.Buy the dip while it's falling: That's buying weakness. Wait for the stock to show strength first.
wrong.Add today with a wider stop: A wider stop makes the add riskier, and the stock is still falling.
wrong.Double up to catch the low: Nobody can call the low. Doubling up before the turn is a guess, sized big.

questions.story: You own 100 shares from $50. It runs to $56 and pulls back. You add 100 at $55 and raise the stop on all 200 to $52.
questions.q: If the stop fills at $52, where does the whole trade end?
questions.why: A $100 loss. Your first 100 shares make money at $52, but the add from $55 loses more. With your first buy still close to the new stop, a stop-out turns the whole trade red.
questions.lesson_line: Before you add, check where the whole position ends if the new stop hits.

wrong.A $200 gain: That counts only your first 100 shares. The add loses money at $52.
wrong.A $300 loss: That counts only the add. Your first 100 shares are in profit at $52.
wrong.Break even: The two lots don't offset here. The add loses more than the first buy makes.

questions.story: You buy 200 shares at $10. It rallies to $12.50, where you sell 100. Then it falls back and your breakeven stop sells the rest at $10.
questions.q: Leaving out commissions, what did the partial do against holding all 200 to that stop?

args.expr: h * (part - entry) + h * (stop - entry) - s * (stop - entry)

questions.why: Made you $250 more. Held as one lot, all 200 shares round-trip to nothing at $10. The partial sold 100 shares at $12.50 before the stock came back. That is the only profit in the trade. Bulkowski's third test found the same: scaling out works better when price falls back to the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Partials pay when the stock comes back. That's what you buy with the upside you give up.

wrong.Made no difference: Holding all 200 made nothing. Your partial at $12.50 was real profit.
wrong.Made you $500 more: Only 100 shares sold at $12.50, not all 200.
wrong.Left you worse off: Backwards. The partial is the only profit in this trade.

questions.simple: It made you $250 more. Holding all 200 to the $10 stop made nothing, while the partial banked a gain.

deeper.trap: Two things hide here. Bulkowski's own numbers include commissions, which is why his gain is $220. And a breakeven stop order is not a promise. Once triggered it fills at market, so a gap through $10 could turn the last 100 shares into a loss.

questions.story: You own 200 shares from $40. It's at $50 and a new setup fires there, with its own stop at $47. You risk $300 per trade.
questions.q: What's the most the add can be?
questions.why: 100 shares. The add is a new trade, so it gets sized from its own stop: $300 of risk over the distance from $50 to $47.
questions.lesson_line: An add gets its own stop and its own size, like any new trade.

wrong.200 shares: That copies your first buy. From this stop it risks double your plan.
wrong.300 shares: That reads your risk dollars as shares. It risks three times your plan.
wrong.None, you already own it: Owning it isn't the test. A new buy point in a winner is a chance to add.

questions.story: Your swing trade is well under your entry and close to your stop. You already bought more once on the way down. You still like the company and want to buy more.
questions.q: Which move fits our plan?
choices: Take the loss and move on
Lower the stop, give it room
Buy more, half size this time
questions.answer: Take the loss and move on
questions.why: Take the loss and move on. Bulkowski's line for swing traders: if you want to average down a second time, sell the loser instead. O'Neil and Hirsch say don't average down at all. Our plan never adds, and the stop only moves up. Your first add already made this position bigger than you planned.
questions.lesson_line: Admit the mistake, take the loss, move on. Liking the company doesn't change the chart.

wrong.Average down one more time: That's the second average down Bulkowski says to swap for a sale. If it keeps falling, the loss gets bigger.
wrong.Lower the stop, give it room: Our stop only moves up, never down or wider. Lowering it widens the loss you planned.
wrong.Buy more, half size this time: Smaller is still adding to a loser. The size doesn't fix the direction.

questions.simple: Take the loss and move on. A second buy on the way down only makes a losing trade bigger.

deeper.trap: Under our rule this trade went wrong at the first add, because we never add. Selling now, or letting the stop take it, both end the trade. The two moves our rule forbids are the ones that feel kindest: buying again and giving the stop room.

reasons: asks what fits our plan (A4, A5)

questions.story: You hold a full position in a leader. It has run hard for two weeks and sits far above its moving averages. Your stop is well below.
questions.q: What's your move?
choices: Sell a portion, trail the rest
Sell all, it can't go higher
questions.answer: Sell a portion, trail the rest
questions.why: Sell a portion, trail the rest. You lock in some of the run while it's strong and keep shares on for more. Our rule: sell some into strength and trail the rest under the rising averages. Hirsch cuts to a two-thirds or even one-third position when a stock is extended short term. Schwab's version: sell a portion and let the remainder ride.
questions.lesson_line: When it's stretched, sell some into strength. Let the rest show how far it can go.

wrong.Add more while it's running: We never add to a position. And buying an extended stock is chasing: O'Neil warns those buys get shaken out on normal pullbacks.
wrong.Lower the stop for room: Our stop only moves up, never down. On a winner, lowering it hands back more of the gain.
wrong.Sell all, it can't go higher: That bets on a top. Our rule sells only some into strength and trails the rest.

questions.simple: Sell part of it and trail the rest. You bank some of the run and keep shares on for more.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading 'extended' as a signal to buy more or to sell everything. For us it is neither. A stretched stock is a place to sell some into strength. Our trims also have set levels: a third at 3R and a third at 5R.

questions.q: Our rule is to buy the full position at one price, with one stop.
questions.why: True. The whole size goes on at one price, with one stop. We don't start with a small piece, and we don't add as it works. What we scale is the exit, never the entry.
questions.lesson_line: Full size, one price, one stop. No adding.
questions.simple: True. We put the whole position on at one price with one stop, and we never add to it.

questions.q: When does our stop move up to breakeven?
questions.why: Once it's 2R to 5R up. Our rule moves the stop to breakeven once the trade is 2R to 5R ahead, ideally. From there the stop only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule.
questions.lesson_line: Stop to breakeven once the trade is 2R to 5R ahead. After that it only moves up, except under the gap rule.

wrong.The day after you buy: Too early. The move comes once the trade is 2R to 5R ahead, not on a date.
wrong.As soon as it's 1R up: Too early for us. Our rule waits until the trade is 2R to 5R ahead.
wrong.Never, it never moves: Our stop never moves down or wider, except under the gap rule. But it does move up: at 2R to 5R it goes to breakeven.

questions.simple: Once it's 2R to 5R up. That is when our rule moves the stop to your entry.

reasons: fixed in final check: key is B19's own window, not the 3R course convention

questions.q: Finish our trim rule.
questions.sentence: At 3R we sell a ___ of the position.
questions.why: A third. Our hard rule is a third at 3R, another third at 5R, and the last third trails a rising average. Ideally the first trim sits anywhere from 3R to 6R. The rule we teach is the hard one: a third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, trail the rest.
questions.simple: A third. At 3R we sell one third, at 5R another third, and the last third trails.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: We enter with a limit order, to control the price we pay.
questions.why: False. Our entries are market orders, not limit orders. When the setup triggers, the buy goes in at market. The order that waits is the stop: a real stop order with the broker, not one kept in your head.
questions.lesson_line: Entries at market. The stop is the order that waits.
questions.simple: False. Our entries are market orders, and the stop order is the one that waits with the broker.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, D41)

questions.q: Entry $50, stop $47.50. Where is the 3R price?
questions.why: One R is the distance from the $50 entry down to the $47.50 stop. Three times that, added above the entry, is the 3R price: $57.50. It is a measuring mark, not an order to sell. When you sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later.
questions.lesson_line: Know the 3R price before you buy. It is a mark on the trade, not a sell order.
questions.simple: $57.50. Three times the gap between your $50 entry and $47.50 stop, added to the entry, is the 3R price.

wrong.$55.00: That is only two times the risk. 3R takes three times it.
wrong.$42.50: Went three times the risk below the entry. 3R sits above it.
wrong.$53.00: Added a flat $3.00, not three times the risk.

questions.q: Entry $80, stop $77. Where is 5R, our second trim?
questions.why: One R is the distance from the $80 entry down to the $77 stop. Five times that, added above the entry, is 5R: $95. That is our second trim. Another third comes off there, and the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: 5R: the second third comes off. The last third trails.
questions.simple: $95. Five times the gap between your $80 entry and $77 stop, added to the entry, is the second trim.

wrong.$85.00: Added a flat $5.00, not five times the risk.
wrong.$92.00: That is only four times the risk. The second trim is at five times.
wrong.$65.00: Went five times the risk below the entry. 5R sits above it.

questions.q: Your last third is trailing. Which line do we trail under, and what makes us sell?
choices: A 10% trailing stop from the high
questions.why: The 10-day or 21-day average, and a close below it. The 10-day suits fast movers, the 21-day steadier ones. An intraday dip under the line is not a sale; a close below it is. The trail follows a moving average, not a fixed percent.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the 10-day or 21-day. A close below it sells the last third.

wrong.The 50-day; any dip below it: Our default lines are the 10-day and 21-day. And a dip isn't a close.
wrong.The 200-day; a close below it: Our default lines are the 10-day for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones, not the 200-day.
wrong.A 10% trailing stop from the high: That's a percent trail. Ours follows a moving average, the 10-day or 21-day, and a close below it sells.

questions.simple: The 10-day or 21-day average. A close below that line sells the last third.

questions.story: You bought at $20 with the stop at $19. By noon on the same day, the stock trades at $23, 3R, on news.
questions.q: What do you do about the first sell?
choices: Hold; he rarely sells on day 1
Sell a third now, it is at 3R
Sell it all, a gain is a gain
Sell half now and lift the stop
questions.answer: Hold; he rarely sells on day 1
questions.why: Hold. He very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy and usually waits until day 3 at the earliest. The 3R price is a mark, not an order to sell. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push is often best. Meanwhile the stop stays where it is.
questions.lesson_line: Rarely sell on day 1. The first sell usually waits until day 3 or later.

wrong.Sell a third now, it is at 3R: That was the old fixed rule. The first sell is a judgment, and he rarely sells on day 1.
wrong.Sell it all, a gain is a gain: That cuts a winner short. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push is often best.
wrong.Sell half now and lift the stop: Day 1 is too early to sell by rule. He usually waits until day 3 at the earliest.

questions.simple: Hold, because he very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy and usually waits until day 3 at the earliest.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, B19)

questions.story: You bought a setup 11 trading days ago. It never hit the stop, but it's only up about half an R and going nowhere.
questions.q: What does our rule say?
choices: Sell it, the time stop hit
Move the stop up to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it, the time stop hit
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold: that is our time stop. This one is about half an R up after 11 trading days, so it goes. The money goes back to work on a setup that is moving. Dead money has a cost even when it never hits the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1R after 10 trading days: sell. Dead money has a cost.

wrong.Hold until the stop or 3R: That is for a trade that moves. After 10 trading days under 1R, the time stop ends it.
wrong.Widen the stop and wait: The stop never moves down or wider. And waiting is the problem here, not the fix.
wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven: Our breakeven move comes at 2R to 5R, and this trade is under 1R. The time stop sells it instead.

questions.simple: Sell it. Our time stop sells any trade still under 1R after 10 trading days.

deeper.trap: The trap is that nothing looks wrong. The stop never hit and the trade is green. But our time stop measures progress, not losses. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, so the money can go to a setup that is moving.

questions.q: A stock gaps down through your stop at the open. Our rule: the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop.
questions.why: True. On a gap down through your stop, the first 30 minutes of the day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. There is a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes already take the loss past 2R, you get out. This is the one exception to our rule that the stop only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop. Past 2R, you're out.
questions.simple: True. When a stock gaps down through your stop, the low of the first 30 minutes becomes the new stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, G70)
open question for the owner: how the broker stop order (D41) meets the gap rule

questions.story: You bought your full size at $30, stop $28.50. It's at $33 and a friend says add half again, it's working.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Add half, it's proving you right
Add half, raise the stop on all
Sell it all and rebuy bigger
questions.why: Add nothing. The whole size went on at $30 with one stop, and we never add. Manage the trade instead. The first sell is a judgment, and he usually waits until day 3 at the earliest. More shares bought higher would only raise what a reversal costs.
questions.lesson_line: Full size at one price. An add is not our trade.

wrong.Add half, it's proving you right: Averaging up is a real method and other traders use it. It isn't ours: the full size went on at one price, with one stop.
wrong.Add half, raise the stop on all: Raising the stop is fine on its own. Adding isn't, and more shares bought higher raise what a reversal costs.
wrong.Sell it all and rebuy bigger: That's an add with extra steps. Our size was set from the stop at the entry.

questions.simple: Add nothing. We buy the full size once, at one price with one stop, and then only manage it.

deeper.counter: Averaging up is a real method. IBD uses later buy points to add to a position it already holds. It isn't ours. Our size is set once, from the stop at the entry, so the risk you planned is the risk you carry.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, B19)

questions.story: You bought 300 shares at $40, stop $38, in one order. By day 5 it has run to $46, 3R, and it sits well above its rising 10-day average.
questions.q: What does our plan do now?
choices: Sell some at $46, trail the rest
Hold all 300 and never sell a share
questions.answer: Sell some at $46, trail the rest
questions.why: Sell some at $46, trail the rest. On a $40 entry with a $38 stop, $46 is 3R, a mark on the trade and not an order. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push is often best, and this is day 5. The rest rides the rising 10-day and sells on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, then a first sell on judgment, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Trail the rest.

wrong.Sell all 300 at $46, one target: That banks everything at one price. We sell some into strength and trail the rest.
wrong.Hold all 300 and never sell a share: That banks nothing into a 5 day push. We sell some into strength and trail the rest.
wrong.Add 100 more shares at $46: We never add. The whole size goes on at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Sell some at $46 and trail the rest, because a 5 day push is a good place for a first sell.

deeper.example: Count it in R. $46 is 3R. It is a mark, not a sell order. The first sell is a judgment into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R. The rest has no target: it rides the 10-day until a close below it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, E52)

conflicts: Shape of the ladder. IBD (s1: add-ons are 'fewer shares than you purchased in the initial breakout') and IBKR (s11: 'successively smaller increments') put the biggest piece first; Investopedia (s7) starts with smaller trade sizes and adds when winning; Bulkowski (s14) says 'I do not buy half a position and then buy another half. I buy a full position' and on a fresh breakout 'I'll double my position.' docs/study/sizing_rule.md section 5 ('Progressive exposure: pilot, half, full, add only after the last step paid') is not marked as the owner's answer or quoted in his words, so it is a lead, not a house source. The file keys only what all of them agree on: add only to a trade that is working, never to a loser; size each add as a new trade; IBD's stated reason for a smaller add (it keeps the average cost down). Settled by the owner, 2026-11-09 (sizing_rule.md section 5 and rule A5): 'I do not scale into trade i buy full at one spot with one stop.' No ladder on the way in is taught as ours; every item that built a position in pieces or added to one is cut (w1, w2, q05, q08, q10, q11, q18, q20, q21, q23).

Investopedia 'Scale In' (s7) contradicts itself: its definition and first example describe buying as the price falls ($20, $19.90, $19.80, $19.70 for a $19.85 average), which is scale trading or averaging down, while its Benefits section describes starting small and adding only when the trade is winning. The file cites only the Benefits lines (f19, f20) and the scale-out lines (f21, f22), and never keys a definition of 'scaling in'.

Does scaling out pay? Bulkowski (s12) and the Howard Bandy study he reports (Active Trader, September 2009) find scaling out lowers profit on trades that run; Dave Mabe, in a third-party post on IBKR Campus ('Exiting Your Trades: What Works Best?', 2025-01-31), says he doesn't scale out 'since you end up paying for the privilege with trading profit'. Schwab (s6), Fidelity / Hirsch (s4), Investopedia (s7, s8) and the owner's own rule (h01) favour selling part into strength. The file teaches it as a trade-off with both halves sourced and calculated (q19: less when the stock runs to target; q22: more when it comes back), never as more profit. The Mabe post is not cited (a third-party blog repost IBKR disclaims).

Bandy's scaling-in study (reported on s14): in a flat 2004 to 2008 market with month-long holds, averaging down ($264 a trade) beat every other test except buy-and-hold with no stops ($1,810). Bulkowski takes issue (gaps, one neutral market). The file never claims averaging down always loses; it keys O'Neil's and Hirsch's rule and the mechanics (a lower average on a bigger position in a falling stock, which still has to turn up).

Bulkowski (s13) allows a swing trader ONE average down when the market and industry are rising, and says sell instead of a second. O'Neil (s3) and Hirsch (s4) say don't average down at all. The file's scenarios key 'don't add' only where all three agree: a stock sliding toward the stop (q12) or a second average down (q24).

Breakeven stops. Investopedia (s7) says moving the stop to breakeven after the first target is common and leaves the rest 'almost risk-free'; Bandy (via s12) found a breakeven stop 'dramatically reduces profit'; FINRA (s17) says a triggered stop fills at market. The file keys that a breakeven stop can still lose money (q16); since 2026-11-09 it also teaches our rule B19 (stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, taught at the first trim, 3R) as ours (q27, q29, q32, q37).

Investopedia 'Pyramiding' (s10) ties pyramiding to margin and leverage and calls it unsuitable for beginners; IBKR's glossary (s11) also says 'as margin'. IBD's add-on buys (s1) need no margin. The file keys only the direction (adding to a position that is working) and never says pyramiding requires margin.

Investopedia 'Average Down' (s9) says that after 100 shares at $60 and 100 at $40 the investor shows 'a 16% profit once the stock hits $60'. On the $50 average that is a 20% gain ($10 / $50); 16.7% is $10 measured on the $60 price. Not used.

Fidelity / Hirsch (s4) 'up 40%, sell 20%' example says it 'leaves you with 125% of the initial position'; the arithmetic is unclear, so it is not used. Only his 'sell half on a double' (q15) and the two-thirds / one-third trim (q25) are cited, as his rules, not ours.

Replaced 2026-11-09. Until today this unit taught the detectors' plan from docs/study/TRADE_PLANS.md: 'Trim is where to take some off: the detectors put the targets at 2R and 3R. They do not say how much to sell at each, so the course names the levels and does not invent a fraction' (q09, q17 keyed 2R and 3R, no fraction). The owner's account rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 9: B19, E51, E52, F63, C33, B20, E57, A5) replaces it: a third at 3R with the stop to breakeven, a third at 5R, the last third trails the 10-day or 21-day and sells on a close below it; TRADE_PLANS.md was rewritten to match the same day. B19 also records that he 'mostly waits for 5R' in practice; the course teaches the hard rule (a third at 3R) and says so.
Investopedia 'Scale Out' (terms/s/scale-out.asp) refused the plain client (403) on 2026-11-09, so it is not cited; the scale-out definition comes from the Scale In page (s7) and Bulkowski (s12).
